vignette:
The Weight of Glass

Marcus is a 57-year-old interior designer who built his career on the belief that spaces should feel safe. His studio in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city is filled with fabric swatches, architectural drawings, and the quiet hum of a man who has spent three decades making other people's environments beautiful. That sense of control - over color, proportion, light - was something he counted on. Eighteen months ago, a highway overpass changed everything.

It was a Tuesday afternoon in November, unremarkable until it wasn't. Marcus was driving back from a client consultation when a commercial truck drifted into his lane on the elevated interchange. The collision sent his car through the guardrail. He remembers the sensation of falling - a long, terrible second of it - before the vehicle landed on the embankment below. He was conscious throughout. He remembers the sound of the windshield splintering, the smell of something burning, and the strange silence that followed before anyone came. He lay pinned for nearly forty minutes, certain he was dying, talking to his adult daughter in his head as though saying goodbye.

He walked away with three broken ribs, a fractured wrist, and a laceration across his left forearm that required surgery. Physically, his doctors told him, he was lucky. Marcus does not feel lucky.

In the weeks that followed the accident, he told himself the jumpiness would pass. It didn't. He stopped taking the highway, then stopped driving entirely, navigating his life through rideshares and apologetic explanations to clients. He began waking at three in the morning with his heart hammering, sometimes unsure whether he had been dreaming or whether the ceiling above him was the inside of a crushed car. The images come without invitation - the guardrail, the glass, the particular gray of the November sky as it tilted sideways. Sometimes they arrive while he is standing in a client's kitchen, measuring counter space, and he has to grip the edge of something solid and breathe until the room comes back.

His marriage had already ended several years before the accident, and he lives alone in an apartment he has not fully furnished, which strikes him as a painful irony he cannot quite laugh at yet. He has become reluctant to invite people over, reluctant to sit near windows, reluctant to take on projects that require him to cross bridges or travel to sites outside the city core. Two long-term clients have quietly moved on. He tells himself he understands.

What troubles Marcus most is how the accident has colonized the work he loves. Interior design requires him to think spatially, to imagine how a person moves through a room, how light enters and changes a space across the hours of a day. Now when he sits at his drafting table, he finds himself calculating exits - where the doors are, how quickly a person could get out. He obsesses over structural details in ways that feel less like professional diligence and more like dread. He has begun avoiding projects in high-rise buildings altogether, telling clients he prefers ground-floor residential work.

He describes himself as "not the same person" who drove to that client meeting in November. He is quieter. He drinks more than he used to - two or three glasses of whiskey most evenings, enough to make sleep feel possible. He has become short-tempered with his daughter when she calls, then floods with guilt afterward and doesn't call back for days. He describes a persistent flatness, an inability to feel pleasure in things that once anchored him - a well-resolved design, a beautiful piece of reclaimed wood, the particular satisfaction of handing a client the keys to a finished room.

He came to therapy, he says, because his daughter asked him to, and because he is frightened by how small his world has become. He sits in the office chair with his arms crossed loosely over his chest, as though still protecting his ribs, and speaks carefully, like a man who has learned that the ground can disappear without warning.
